questions.evidence:
During a group project, the teacher asks students to prepare a short talk about a local landmark. Half the group nods while the instructions are read. Everyone looks busy afterward, but their notes do not match when they meet at the end of the period.

Sora has researched the landmark's history. Tim has drawn a detailed map of every bus stop nearby. Mei has written a speech about her favorite restaurant beside it. Each student believed a different detail was the most important part of the assignment.

The group rereads the task card. It asks for the landmark's history, why residents value it, and one practical visiting tip. They can use Sora's research, shorten Tim's map to one useful route, and ask Mei to interview a resident instead.

Before dividing the remaining work, each student repeats their task in their own words. They agree on a two-minute limit for the whole talk. Nodding was quick, but checking a shared understanding turns out to save more time.

Let each student give a separate two-minute talk.
